title: Marginal Tax Rates
summary: SHELVES → MARGINAL RATE → EFFECTIVE RATE → DECIDE
subtitle: You get offered more money, and a voice in your head says you might end up with less. You won’t.

blocks.text: You get offered more money. A promotion, a new job, a bonus.
And somewhere in the back of your mind, a voice says: wait, won’t this push me into a higher bracket? Won’t I end up with less? No. You won’t.
That fear comes from a mix-up about marginal tax rates, and it talks people out of raises, promotions and side income every year. This lesson puts it to rest for good.
Say yes to more money with confidence, because you’ll know what it is worth.
blocks.detail: Once you see how the shelves work, you can price a raise, overtime or a side gig in minutes instead of guessing.
blocks.extra: Section 04 runs the numbers on a real salary.

sections.title: Picture shelves, not a single price tag

blocks.text: Forget the word bracket for a second. Picture shelves instead.
Your income gets stacked onto shelves, starting from the bottom. Each shelf has its own tax rate. The bottom shelf has the lowest rate. Each shelf above it costs a little more.
Here’s the part that matters most: a shelf’s tax rate applies only to the income sitting on that shelf. Not your whole income. Just that slice.

When someone says “I’m in the 20.5% bracket,” they don’t mean 20.5% of everything they earn. They mean their top dollars, the ones on that shelf, are taxed at that rate. Every dollar below is still taxed at the lower rates of the shelves underneath.
Here’s what the federal shelves look like for 2026.
Federal tax shelves, 2026

items.title: Up to $58,523
items.text: 14% — on the first $58,523 of taxable income.

items.title: $58,523 to $117,045
items.text: 20.5% — on the slice between these two amounts.

items.title: $117,045 to $181,440
items.text: 26% — on the slice between these two amounts.

items.title: $181,440 to $258,482
items.text: 29% — on the slice between these two amounts.

blocks.text: Your province stacks its own shelves on top of these, at its own rates. Your combined marginal rate is the federal rate plus the provincial rate on your top dollar. That’s why take-home pay differs across provinces at the same salary. The CRA lists every province’s rates on its website.

The shelves apply to taxable income, not your salary. Deductions such as RRSP contributions, union dues and child care costs come off first, so less of your income reaches the higher shelves. Credits, like the Basic Personal Amount, work differently: they cut the tax itself after it is worked out.

items.title: “If I earn $60,000, all of it gets taxed at 20.5% because that’s my bracket.”
items.text: Only about $1,500 of it does, the sliver above $58,523. The other $58,523 is still taxed at 14%, the same as someone earning exactly that amount. Your bracket describes your last dollar, never your whole income.

blocks.text: Numbers beat explanations. Here’s someone with $70,000 of taxable income in 2026, federal tax only.

items.title: First $58,523, taxed at 14%. That’s $8,193.22.
Remaining $11,477, taxed at 20.5%. That’s $2,352.79.
Total federal tax: $10,546.01, before any credits.

blocks.text: Notice what didn’t happen. The whole $70,000 was not taxed at 20.5%. Only the top slice was. That’s the entire idea, in one example.
CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: MARGINAL RATE VS. EFFECTIVE RATE

In that example, the marginal rate is 20.5%. That’s the rate on the next dollar earned, the one that matters for overtime or a side gig. The effective rate, total tax divided by total income, is about 15%. That’s the share of the whole income that went to tax. Both numbers are real, and they answer different questions. Marginal rate answers “What happens if I earn one more dollar?” Effective rate answers “Overall, what share did I pay?” Mixing them up is where the raise-anxiety myth comes from.

sections.title: Where this actually changes a decision

blocks.text: Your marginal rate isn’t trivia. It’s the number behind several real money choices.

RRSP contributions. An RRSP contribution lowers your taxable income, so it saves tax at your marginal rate, the rate on your top shelf. Someone on the 29% shelf saves more per dollar than someone on the 14% shelf. That’s why RRSP contributions are often worth more in your highest-earning years.
A raise or a bonus. Once you know only your top slice moves to a new rate, the worry mostly fades. A raise that pushes a sliver of income onto a higher shelf still leaves you with more money overall.

A side gig or freelance income. Extra income stacks on top of what you already earn. If your day job already fills your lower shelves, side income often lands on a higher shelf right away. Set some aside, so a tax bill doesn’t surprise you the next spring.

Watch for benefits that shrink as income grows. Income-tested payments, like the Canada Child Benefit, the GST/HST credit and the Canada Workers Benefit, get smaller as your family income rises. Add that to your tax rate and a raise can keep less than you expect. You still come out ahead, but if you get these benefits, count them when you weigh extra work.

items.title: “Everyone should max out their RRSP as early as possible to save on tax.”
items.text: The tax saving is bigger in years you sit on a higher shelf. In a lower-earning year, like a first job or a parental leave, you may get more value by saving the room and contributing later, once your income and marginal rate have climbed. Timing the contribution can matter as much as the amount.

sections.title: Before you turn down extra income out of tax fear

items.title: I know which shelf my current income mostly sits on.
I understand that only new income above my current shelf moves to a higher rate.
I know my marginal rate is not the same as my effective rate.
I won’t confuse a raise with a pay cut. A raise leaves me with more, never less.
I’ve checked my province’s shelves too, since the full picture includes both.

blocks.text: Renata almost said no
paragraphs: Renata worked as a receptionist in a dental office in Halifax. She had been saving for a used car so she could stop taking two buses to work every morning. Then her manager offered her a promotion to office lead, with her salary going from $55,000 to $62,000.

That Sunday, over dinner, her uncle shook his head. A raise like that could bump her into a higher tax bracket, he warned, and she might end up taking home less. He meant well, and he sounded completely certain.

Renata lay awake that night doing sums in the dark. The new job meant more hours and more stress, and if it also meant less money, there was no point. On Monday morning she drafted a polite note turning it down.
Before she sent it, she decided to check one thing. She asked Kofi, a coworker who had made a similar jump the year before, and he grabbed a napkin in the lunchroom and drew a set of shelves.

Only the $3,477 above $58,523 would move up to the 20.5% shelf, he showed her. Everything below that line kept its 14% rate. Her uncle had mixed up the rate on her last few dollars with the rate on all of them.

Renata deleted the note and took the promotion. Her pay went up, though not by the full $7,000, since the top slice was taxed a little more. By spring she was driving her used car to work, and the napkin was folded in the glove box.

blocks.text: Tax brackets work like shelves. Only the income on a shelf is taxed at that shelf’s rate, and everything below keeps its lower rate. Your marginal rate is the rate on your next dollar. Your effective rate is your overall average. A raise never leaves you with less money, even if a slice of it lands on a higher shelf.
Weigh every money decision by the rate on your next dollar.

blocks.text: Worksheet: know your own shelves

items.title: Marginal tax rate
items.text: The rate on your next dollar of income. Describes only your top shelf.

items.title: Effective tax rate
items.text: Your total tax divided by your total income. Your overall average.

items.title: Tax bracket
items.text: A range of income taxed at one rate. A higher bracket never applies to income below it.

items.title: Taxable income
items.text: Your income after deductions, like RRSP contributions, come off. This is what the shelves apply to.

blocks.text: Educational only, not tax advice. Figures shown are 2026 rates. Confirm your own province and year before relying on any number here.

questions: About how much taxable income will you have this year?
Which federal shelf does your top dollar sit on?
What is your combined marginal rate, federal plus provincial?
Did your marginal and effective rates feel like the same thing before this lesson?
Do you get any benefits that shrink as your income rises?
What decision have you put off because of tax fear, and does the shelf idea change it?
